passage.title: The Transformation of Education through Artificial Intelligence
passage.text:
The proposition that artificial intelligence will fundamentally transform formal education is, by 2026, no longer a speculative claim advanced by technology enthusiasts on the margins of pedagogical discourse — it is an observable institutional reality whose consequences educators, policymakers, and cognitive scientists are racing to characterize with sufficient precision to inform consequential decisions about curriculum design, assessment architecture, and the allocation of public educational investment. The transformation, however, is neither uniform in its manifestations nor unambiguous in its implications. It is unfolding across educational contexts of radically different resource endowments, pedagogical traditions, and institutional cultures in ways that resist the totalizing narratives — of either utopian disruption or civilizational risk — that dominate popular commentary on the subject. [1] What the available evidence supports, with growing but still incomplete confidence, is a more differentiated account: that AI's educational impact is deeply conditioned by the quality of its implementation, the pedagogical intentions that govern its deployment, and the institutional capacity of educational systems to manage a transition for which few were structurally prepared.

The most theoretically consequential debate surrounding AI in education concerns not its operational utility — the efficiency gains in administrative processing, the personalization of formative assessment feedback, the reduction of routine grading burden on teaching staff — but its relationship to the development of the cognitive capacities that education has historically been understood to cultivate. The concern, articulated with particular clarity by developmental psychologists working in the Vygotskian tradition, is that the habitual offloading of cognitively demanding tasks to AI systems during the formative years of intellectual development may interfere with the construction of the mental schemas, metacognitive strategies, and tolerance for productive struggle that constitute the deep architecture of expert thinking. This is not a concern about surface-level academic dishonesty — the substitution of AI-generated text for student-authored work — but about a more subtle and potentially more consequential developmental risk: that students who never experience the sustained effort of generating extended reasoning independently may arrive at cognitive adulthood with impoverished capacities that no subsequent remediation can fully restore. [2]

The counterargument, advanced with equal theoretical sophistication by researchers working in the cognitive tools tradition derived from the work of Gavriel Salomon, holds that the relevant question is not whether AI performs cognitive work that students would otherwise perform themselves, but whether the human-AI cognitive partnership produces outcomes — in understanding, transfer, and the capacity for further independent learning — that exceed what either party could achieve alone. On this view, the capacity to direct, interrogate, and critically evaluate AI-generated reasoning is itself a high-order cognitive achievement whose cultivation represents a legitimate and demanding educational objective. The student who learns to identify the logical gap in an AI-produced argument, to recognize the ideological assumption embedded in an AI-generated historical narrative, or to detect the statistical artifact masquerading as a causal claim in an AI-synthesized research summary is engaging in precisely the kind of critical epistemic practice that sophisticated education has always sought to develop — through different tools, in different historical moments. [3]

The equity implications of differential AI access in educational settings have received comparatively less analytical attention than the cognitive development debate, despite representing arguably the more urgent policy challenge in the near term. The asymmetry is stark: the AI tutoring platforms that have demonstrated the most robust learning gains in controlled experimental conditions — those that provide adaptive, personalized instructional scaffolding calibrated to individual students' zone of proximal development — are precisely the systems least accessible to students in under-resourced educational environments. [4] A student in a well-funded private school who engages daily with a sophisticated AI tutoring system from the early years of secondary education accumulates a compounding cognitive and academic advantage over a peer in an underfunded public school whose AI interactions are limited to the free-tier features of general-purpose language models — features whose pedagogical design is optimized for broad accessibility rather than for the kind of deep adaptive instruction that produces durable learning gains. The risk is not merely that AI widens the achievement gap between advantaged and disadvantaged students but that it does so through a mechanism that is largely invisible to the conventional metrics by which educational equity is tracked and evaluated.

Assessment represents the institutional domain in which AI's transformative pressure has been felt most acutely and responded to most visibly. The capacity of large language models to generate text that is indistinguishable from competent student writing across a wide range of genres and disciplines has rendered the take-home written assignment — the workhorse of formative and summative assessment in higher education for more than a century — functionally compromised as a measure of individual student ability. Institutional responses have varied widely, from outright prohibition policies that are widely acknowledged to be unenforceable, to the redesign of assessment toward oral examination, in-class performance, and portfolio-based evaluation, to the explicit integration of AI as a collaborative tool within assessed tasks accompanied by requirements for critical reflection on the AI's contribution. Each of these responses carries its own pedagogical logic and its own set of unresolved tensions, and no consensus has emerged among assessment researchers about which approach best balances the competing imperatives of academic integrity, equitable access, and the development of the competencies that AI-augmented professional practice will actually require.

The implications for the teaching profession itself are among the least examined but potentially most significant dimensions of educational AI transformation. The automation of routine assessment feedback, curriculum resource curation, and administrative documentation — tasks that collectively consume a substantial portion of teaching time in most educational systems — creates the theoretical possibility of liberating teachers for the high-value relational, diagnostic, and motivational work that research consistently identifies as the most consequential determinant of student outcomes. Whether this possibility is realized in practice depends, however, on institutional decisions about whether the time freed by AI automation is reinvested in teacher-student interaction or extracted as a productivity gain through staff reduction — a decision that reflects institutional values and resource priorities rather than any property of the technology itself.

The longer-term question of how AI reshapes the very definition of educational attainment — what it means to be educated, what knowledge and capabilities confer genuine human advantage in an AI-augmented world, and how formal educational credentials can credibly signal the possession of those capabilities to employers, institutions, and society — remains genuinely open in ways that current educational systems are not yet structurally equipped to address. The historical function of formal education as the primary mechanism for the intergenerational transmission of validated knowledge is being challenged by AI systems whose knowledge breadth vastly exceeds any individual teacher's and whose availability is not bounded by institutional schedules or geographic access constraints. What education retains that AI cannot replicate — the cultivation of judgment, the development of ethical reasoning, the formation of intellectual identity, and the irreducibly social process of becoming a thinking member of a community of practice — may ultimately constitute the most defensible rationale for the continued investment of public resources in formal educational institutions. Whether educational systems can reorient themselves around these distinctively human capacities, rather than continuing to optimize for the transmission of information that AI has rendered abundantly and freely available, is the defining institutional challenge of the coming generation.

The honest assessment of AI's educational transformation in 2026 is that it is simultaneously more consequential and less tractable than either its most ardent proponents or its most alarmed critics have been willing to acknowledge. The institutions, educators, and policymakers who will navigate it most successfully are likely to be those who resist the temptation of both uncritical adoption and reflexive prohibition — and who instead invest in the slow, evidence-driven, contextually sensitive work of understanding what AI makes possible, what it makes more difficult, and what it leaves unchanged in the fundamentally human project of learning to think well.

tasks.suggestion:
Để đạt kết quả tốt cho phần thi này, bạn nên áp dụng các chiến thuật sau đây:

  • Dạng câu hỏi Ý chính & Thái độ tác giả (R4Q1, R4Q9): Sử dụng kỹ năng Skimming (Đọc lướt). Đọc đoạn mở đầu và đoạn kết luận (đoạn 8) để nắm cấu trúc toàn bài. Với R4Q1, bài viết bác bỏ các câu chuyện phiến diện một chiều (như chỉ ca ngợi hay chỉ lo ngại gian lận) để đưa ra lập luận trung tâm: tác động của AI không đồng đều mà phụ thuộc vào chất lượng thực thi, ý định sư phạm và năng lực quản lý của thể chế. Với R4Q9, dựa vào việc tác giả khuyên nên tránh cả sự áp dụng mù quáng lẫn cấm đoán rập khuôn ở đoạn 8, ta xác định được tác giả có thái độ cân bằng mang tính phân tích và khiêm tốn về mặt nhận thức ("analytically balanced and epistemically humble"), nhìn nhận vấn đề một cách đa chiều.
  • Dạng câu hỏi Chi tiết (R4Q2, R4Q4, R4Q5, R4Q6): Sử dụng kỹ năng Scanning (Đọc quét) để tìm vùng thông tin dựa trên từ khóa cốt lõi. Với R4Q2, quét đoạn 2 tìm từ khóa "Vygotskian tradition" để làm rõ sự khác biệt: lo ngại của họ không nằm ở việc gian lận bề mặt mà nằm ở nguy cơ tiềm ẩn khi học sinh né tránh các nhiệm vụ tư duy khó, dẫn đến suy giảm năng lực tư duy sâu sắc khó hồi phục. Với R4Q4, quét đoạn 4 tìm từ khóa "achievement gap" hoặc "equity" để thấy cơ chế gây bất bình đẳng: học sinh trường giàu được dùng nền tảng gia sư AI thích ứng hóa cá nhân cao, trong khi trường nghèo chỉ được dùng công cụ miễn phí phổ thông ít hiệu quả hơn. Với R4Q5, rà soát đoạn 5 bàn về các phản ứng trước khủng hoảng kiểm tra để tìm phương án NOT mentioned; bài đọc nhắc đến cấm đoán, đổi sang thi vấn đáp/portfolio, và tích hợp AI làm công cụ cộng tác. Việc bắt buộc viết bài trong phòng thi giám sát có phần mềm quét AI thời gian thực không được nhắc tới. Với R4Q6, quét đoạn 6 tìm từ khóa "teaching profession" để thấy điều kiện để việc tự động hóa có lợi cho học sinh là khi thể chế quyết định tái đầu tư khoảng thời gian trống đó vào các hoạt động tương tác, chẩn đoán và thúc đẩy động lực giữa thầy và trò.
  • Dạng câu hỏi Từ vựng trong ngữ cảnh (R4Q3, R4Q7): Sử dụng kỹ năng Context Clues (Manh mối ngữ cảnh). Với R4Q3, từ "offloading" ở đoạn 2 đi kèm với "habitual offloading... to AI systems" (thói quen offloading sang hệ thống AI) làm mất đi nỗ lực tư duy độc lập, mang nghĩa là chuyển giao hoàn toàn công việc nhận thức cho máy làm thay để né tránh nỗ lực tư duy tự thân. Với R4Q7, từ "tractable" ở đoạn 8 nằm trong cấu trúc song hành "more consequential and less tractable" (hệ quả lớn hơn nhưng ít tractable hơn) dùng để mô tả bản chất của cuộc chuyển đổi AI, mang nghĩa là có thể kiểm soát, quản lý hoặc giải quyết một cách hiệu quả.
  • Dạng câu hỏi Quy chiếu (R4Q8): Đọc kỹ câu chứa cụm từ và câu đứng ngay trước nó ở đoạn 3. Cụm từ "On this view" (Theo quan điểm này) nằm ngay đầu câu 2, dùng để tiếp nối và quy chiếu trực tiếp đến lập luận của trường phái nghiên cứu "công cụ nhận thức" (cognitive tools) của Gavriel Salomon vừa được đưa ra ở câu 1, khẳng định sự cộng tác người-máy có thể tạo ra kết quả học tập vượt trội.
  • Dạng câu hỏi Chèn câu (R4Q10): Câu cần chèn thảo luận về "giới hạn của nghiên cứu thực nghiệm trong việc phân định tranh chấp do khó cô lập đóng góp của AI với các biến số khác". Vị trí [2] ở cuối đoạn 2 là chính xác nhất, vì đoạn 2 vừa trình bày xong lo ngại của phái Vygotskian, câu chèn đóng vai trò là một bước đệm thừa nhận sự khó khăn khi chứng minh lo ngại này bằng thực tế trước khi bài viết chuyển sang đoạn 3 để giới thiệu một phản luận (counterargument) đối lập.

Lời khuyên: Đây là bài đọc có cấu trúc đối lập luận điểm rất rõ ràng (Đoạn 2 lo ngại tư duy đối lập với Đoạn 3 ủng hộ tư duy công cụ). Hãy làm tốt các câu Chi tiết (R4Q2, R4Q4, R4Q5, R4Q6) và câu Từ vựng (R4Q3, R4Q7) bằng cách bám sát văn bản. Sau khi nắm được mạch phản biện giữa hai trường phái ở đoạn 2 và 3, bạn sẽ xử lý câu Chèn câu (R4Q10) và câu Quy chiếu (R4Q8) rất nhanh, từ đó dễ dàng chốt đáp án cho câu hỏi tổng thể về Ý chính (R4Q1) và Thái độ (R4Q9).

questions.question: What is the central argument of the passage?
options: AI's integration into formal education represents an unambiguous improvement over traditional pedagogical approaches because its capacity for personalized adaptive instruction exceeds what any human teacher can deliver at scale across diverse student populations.

AI will ultimately undermine the institutional rationale for formal education by making the knowledge transmission function of schools and universities redundant, leaving only the social and relational dimensions of learning as the defensible justification for continued public investment.

AI's educational transformation is real and consequential but neither uniformly beneficial nor uniformly harmful, with its actual impact determined by implementation quality, pedagogical intention, and institutional capacity rather than by the technology's intrinsic properties.

The primary challenge posed by AI to formal education is the threat it represents to academic integrity, as the capacity of language models to generate student-quality writing has rendered conventional written assessment fundamentally unreliable as a measure of individual ability.

questions.question: According to the passage, what distinguishes the concern raised by developmental psychologists in the Vygotskian tradition from the more commonly discussed problem of academic dishonesty?
options: Developmental psychologists argue that AI poses a greater threat to students in early primary education than to those in secondary or higher education, because the foundational cognitive schemas formed in early childhood are more vulnerable to disruption by technological mediation.

The concern is that AI-generated academic work is of such consistently high quality that it raises the average standard of submitted work across educational institutions, making it impossible for teachers to accurately assess genuine student ability using conventional marking criteria.

Developmental psychologists are concerned primarily with the impact of AI on teacher workload and professional identity, arguing that the automation of assessment feedback deprives teachers of the evaluative practice that maintains and develops their pedagogical expertise.

The Vygotskian concern is not about students submitting AI-generated work as their own but about the subtler developmental risk that students who habitually avoid cognitively demanding tasks may develop impoverished thinking capacities that remediation cannot fully restore.

questions.question: The word "offloading" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to _______.
options: collaborating on cognitively demanding tasks by distributing intellectual labor between human students and AI systems in ways that enhance the quality and sophistication of the final output produced

restructuring cognitively demanding tasks so that they can be completed more efficiently through a combination of human creativity and AI processing capacity without reducing the total cognitive engagement required
selecting which cognitively demanding tasks to complete independently and which to delegate to AI assistance based on a student's assessment of their own current competence and developmental needs

transferring cognitively demanding tasks to AI systems rather than performing them independently, thereby avoiding the sustained mental effort that would otherwise drive the development of relevant cognitive capacities

questions.question: According to the passage, through what specific mechanism does differential AI access risk widening the educational achievement gap between advantaged and disadvantaged students?
options: Students in disadvantaged schools are more likely to use AI tools to complete assessed work dishonestly, while students in well-resourced schools are guided by teachers to use AI as a legitimate learning tool, creating a differential in the quality of academic skills developed through AI interaction.

Students with access to sophisticated adaptive AI tutoring platforms accumulate compounding cognitive and academic advantages through daily personalized instruction, while peers whose access is limited to general-purpose free-tier tools receive pedagogically inferior interactions that produce less durable learning gains.

Students in well-resourced schools gain access to AI systems that automate their homework and exam preparation, while students in under-resourced schools must complete the same tasks without technological assistance, creating a workload disparity that disadvantages less privileged students.

AI grading and feedback systems deployed in well-resourced schools provide students with more detailed and actionable formative assessment information than the feedback available to students in under-resourced schools, accelerating the academic development of already advantaged learners.

questions.question: According to the passage, which of the following institutional responses to AI's impact on assessment is NOT mentioned in the passage?
options: Redesigning assessment toward oral examination, in-class performance tasks, and portfolio-based evaluation formats
Outright prohibition policies that restrict student access to AI tools during the completion of assessed work
Requiring students to complete all assessed writing in supervised examination conditions with AI detection software monitoring submissions in real time
Explicitly integrating AI as a collaborative tool within assessed tasks with requirements for critical reflection on its contribution

questions.question: According to the passage, under what condition would the time freed by AI automation of routine teaching tasks most likely benefit students rather than reduce staffing costs?
options: When governments establish minimum staffing ratios that prevent educational institutions from reducing teacher headcount as a consequence of AI automation, protecting the human relational dimensions of teaching from being displaced by efficiency imperatives.

When institutional decisions reinvest the time liberated by AI automation back into teacher-student relational, diagnostic, and motivational interactions rather than extracting it as a productivity gain through staff reduction.

When teachers are given autonomy to determine which of their routine tasks should be automated by AI and which should remain under human control, ensuring that the technology serves pedagogical rather than administrative priorities.

When educational institutions invest the freed time in providing teachers with professional development in AI literacy, enabling them to guide students more effectively in the critical evaluation of AI-generated content and arguments.

questions.question: The word "tractable" in paragraph 8 is closest in meaning to _______.
options: transparent in its mechanisms and effects, allowing educators and policymakers to observe and measure its impact on student learning outcomes through conventional research and evaluation methods

consistent across different educational contexts and implementation conditions, producing predictable outcomes that allow institutions to plan AI integration with reasonable confidence about the results it will generate

significant in its implications for educational policy and practice, carrying consequences that extend beyond the immediate institutional context to shape the longer-term development of educational systems at the national and international level
capable of being effectively managed, addressed, or resolved through deliberate analytical and institutional effort applied with sufficient knowledge and resources

questions.question: The phrase "On this view" in paragraph 3 refers to _______.
options: the argument advanced by researchers in the cognitive tools tradition, who hold that the relevant question is whether human-AI cognitive partnerships produce superior outcomes to what either party could achieve independently

the perspective of educational policymakers who argue that the equity implications of differential AI access represent a more urgent policy challenge than the cognitive development concerns raised by academic researchers

the author's own assessment of AI's educational impact, which treats both the cognitive development concern and the equity challenge as symptoms of a more fundamental failure of institutional preparation and pedagogical intentionality

the position of developmental psychologists working in the Vygotskian tradition, who argue that habitual AI use during formative intellectual development interferes with the construction of the deep cognitive capacities that constitute expert thinking

questions.question: Which of the following best characterizes the author's overall assessment of AI's transformation of formal education as expressed in paragraph 8?
options: Fundamentally skeptical, as the author implies that the cognitive development risks identified by Vygotskian researchers and the equity implications of differential AI access together constitute sufficient grounds for institutional caution about further AI integration in educational settings.

Analytically balanced and epistemically humble, as the author acknowledges that AI's educational consequences are more consequential and less resolvable than either enthusiastic advocates or alarmed critics have been willing to accept, and advocates a slow evidence-driven approach to navigating the transition.

Implicitly critical of educational institutions, as the author suggests that the failure of schools and universities to develop coherent AI governance frameworks reflects a systemic unwillingness to engage seriously with the evidence on AI's pedagogical implications.

Cautiously optimistic, as the author treats the evidence of personalized learning gains from adaptive AI platforms and the liberation of teacher time from routine tasks as sufficient grounds for confidence that AI's educational impact will be net positive for most students.

questions.question: Which of the following square brackets [1], [2], [3], or [4] best indicates where the following sentence could be added? 'The possibility of resolving this dispute through empirical research alone is limited by the methodological difficulty of isolating AI's contribution to cognitive development from the many other variables that shape learning trajectories.'
